slides.title: What is a lemonade stand?
slides.text: A lemonade stand is a tiny business you run. You make lemonade and sell it on hot days.

slides.title: What is trading?
slides.text: Trading means giving something and getting something back. You give lemonade, and get a coin back.

slides.title: Where ideas come from
slides.text: Big ideas start with noticing what people need. You see thirsty people, so you sell cold drinks.

slides.title: Who is a customer?
slides.text: A customer is someone who buys from you. Being kind makes customers want to come back.

slides.title: You can make things too!
slides.text: Making things to sell makes you an entrepreneur. You could make bracelets, drawings, or yummy cookies.

slides.title: It takes effort
slides.text: Running a lemonade stand takes real work. You squeeze lemons and make a sign too.

slides.title: Making something to sell
slides.text: You must make lemonade before you sell it. First mix lemons, sugar, and cold water.

slides.title: A happy customer comes back
slides.text: Happy customers often come back to buy more. Your neighbor loved it, so she came back.

slides.title: Picking a fair price
slides.text: A fair price is not too high or low. One dollar for a cold cup feels fair.

slides.title: Telling people about your stand
slides.text: You can tell people your stand is open. A big colorful sign helps people notice you.

slides.title: Saving up for supplies
slides.text: You can save coins to buy more lemons. Saving a little each day adds up fast.

slides.title: Teamwork with a friend
slides.text: Two friends can run a stand together. One friend pours the cups, and one collects coins.

quiz.question: What is a lemonade stand?
choices: A tiny business selling lemonade
A place to take a nap
quiz.explanation: A lemonade stand is a simple, real example of running a tiny business.

quiz.question: What is a customer?
choices: Someone who buys what you're selling
A type of lemon
quiz.explanation: Customers are the people who buy from your business.

quiz.question: You give lemonade, and get a coin. What just happened?
choices: You traded — you both gave and got something
Nothing happened at all
quiz.explanation: Trading is a fair swap — giving something, getting something back.

quiz.question: Where do business ideas often come from?
choices: Noticing something people want or need
They only come from grown-ups, never kids
quiz.explanation: Great business ideas often start by noticing a want or need, like being thirsty on a hot day.

quiz.question: Does running a lemonade stand take effort?
choices: Yes, it takes real work
No, it happens by itself
quiz.explanation: From squeezing lemons to making a sign, a lemonade stand takes real effort to run.

quiz.question: What must you do before selling lemonade?
choices: Make it first, with lemons, sugar, and water
You can sell it before it exists
quiz.explanation: Making the lemonade comes before selling it — you need something real to offer.

quiz.question: What happens when a customer loves your lemonade?
choices: They often come back to buy more
They never think about it again
quiz.explanation: A happy customer is likely to return, which helps a little business keep going.

quiz.question: What makes a price fair?
choices: Not too high and not too low
As high as you can possibly charge
quiz.explanation: A fair price feels okay to both you and the customer buying from you.

quiz.question: Why make a big sign for your stand?
choices: So people notice your stand and stop by
To keep the sun off your lemonade
quiz.explanation: Telling people your stand is open helps more customers find you.

quiz.question: Two friends run a lemonade stand. What's a good way to work together?
choices: Share the jobs, like pouring cups and collecting coins
One friend does nothing at all
quiz.explanation: Splitting up the jobs makes running a stand easier for both friends.

slides.title: Spotting a problem to solve
slides.text: Good business ideas often start when you notice a problem, like no cold drinks at the park. That kind of gap, noticed on a hot day, could become your very own business idea.

slides.title: Cost vs. price
slides.text: Cost is what it takes to make something, and price is what you charge to sell it. If lemonade costs 20 cents to make and sells for a dollar, your profit is 80 cents.

slides.title: A simple plan
slides.text: Before starting, it helps to plan what you'll sell, what it costs, and what you'll charge. Writing down a plan, like charging a dollar for 20-cent lemonade, avoids confusion later.

slides.title: Good customer service
slides.text: Being friendly, honest, and helpful makes people want to buy from you again. When a customer asks for less sugar and you happily make it their way, they often return.

slides.title: Telling people about it
slides.text: Even a great product needs people to know it exists, which is called marketing. A bright poster that says "Cold Lemonade, $1!" lets passing neighbors know your stand is open.

slides.title: Keeping track
slides.text: Writing down what you spend and earn helps you see if your business is really working. If you spent $4 on supplies and earned $12, you made an $8 profit.

slides.title: Trying again if it doesn't work
slides.text: When a business idea doesn't work at first, entrepreneurs usually adjust it instead of quitting. If nobody stopped by on a cloudy day, you might try a sunnier spot next time.

slides.title: Making your product special
slides.text: Adding something unique, like a flavor nobody else has, can make customers choose your stand. A splash of strawberry or mint, something other stands don't offer, could set you apart.

slides.title: Planning your day
slides.text: Deciding when to open and how much to make ahead of time helps your day run smoothly. Planning to open from 2 to 4pm with 20 cups ready means you won't scramble later.

slides.title: Handling an unhappy customer
slides.text: Sometimes a customer isn't happy, maybe your lemonade seemed too sour for their taste. Listening calmly and offering a new cup, or their money back, keeps their trust.

slides.title: Splitting jobs with a partner
slides.text: Running a business with a friend works best when you split up the jobs. One person could make the lemonade while the other greets customers and handles the money.

slides.title: Saving up for a goal
slides.text: Saving some of your profit each week can help you buy something bigger later on. If you save $2 every week, you'll have $20 saved after ten weeks.

slides.title: Checking what others charge
slides.text: Before setting your price, it helps to check what other nearby sellers are charging. Charging close to their price, or a little less, can help customers choose you.

quiz.question: What does it mean to "spot a problem" for a business idea?
choices: Noticing something people need that isn't available
Finding a hole in your sock
quiz.explanation: Great business ideas often start by noticing a real need that isn't being met.

quiz.question: A cup of lemonade costs 20 cents to make and sells for $1. What is your profit on that cup?
choices: 80 cents
quiz.explanation: Profit is what's left over after you subtract the cost from the price you charged: $1.00 - $0.20 = $0.80.

quiz.question: Why is a simple plan helpful before starting a business?
choices: It helps you figure out what to sell and for how much
Plans are only for grown-ups
quiz.explanation: A simple plan helps you think through what you'll sell, what it costs, and what to charge.

quiz.question: Why does good customer service matter?
choices: It makes customers want to come back and tell friends
It has no real effect on a business
quiz.explanation: Friendly, helpful service builds trust and brings customers back.

quiz.question: What is marketing, in simple terms?
choices: Telling people about what you're selling
Counting your money at the end of the day
quiz.explanation: Marketing is simply letting people know your product or service exists.

quiz.question: If a business idea doesn't work at first, what do entrepreneurs usually do?
choices: Tweak the idea and try again
Never attempt anything again
quiz.explanation: Adjusting and retrying is a normal, healthy part of entrepreneurship.

quiz.question: How can adding a unique flavor to your lemonade help your business?
choices: It can make customers pick you over other sellers
It never makes any difference
quiz.explanation: Something unique about your product gives customers a reason to choose you.

quiz.question: Why is it helpful to plan your day before opening a stand?
choices: It helps the whole day run more smoothly
Planning ahead never actually helps
quiz.explanation: Knowing what supplies and timing you need ahead of time avoids scrambling later.

quiz.question: A customer says your lemonade is too sour. What should you do?
choices: Listen calmly and offer a new cup or their money back
Ignore them and walk away
quiz.explanation: Handling complaints calmly and fairly helps keep a customer's trust.

quiz.question: You and a friend run a stand together. What's a smart way to split the work?
choices: One makes lemonade while the other handles customers and money
Both do the exact same job at the exact same time
quiz.explanation: Splitting up different jobs usually makes a small team more efficient.

quiz.question: If you save $2 every week, how much will you have after 10 weeks?
quiz.explanation: Saving a little bit regularly adds up over time: $2 x 10 weeks = $20.

slides.title: Profit and loss
slides.text: If you earn more than you spend, that's a profit. If you spend more than you earn, that's a loss. Tracking both helps a business survive. For example, if your dog-walking side business earns $60 in a month but spent $75 on flyers, leashes, and treats, that month was actually a $15 loss, even though $60 sounds like good money.

slides.title: Knowing your customer
slides.text: Successful businesses understand who they're selling to — what that person likes, needs, and is willing to pay for. For example, if you're selling handmade bookmarks, knowing that your customers are mostly classmates who love a specific book series could help you design bookmarks featuring those characters, which they'd be far more excited to buy.

slides.title: Teamwork in business
slides.text: Many businesses run better with a team — different people handling different jobs, like making the product, selling it, and managing money. For example, if you and a friend start a dog-walking business together, one of you could focus on finding new customers while the other tracks the schedule and money — splitting the work makes it easier to grow.

slides.title: Taking a smart risk
slides.text: Starting a business always involves some risk — it might not work. Smart entrepreneurs take risks they can afford, not risks that could ruin them. For example, spending $10 of your own savings to try selling friendship bracelets at a school fair is a smart, affordable risk — spending your entire year's savings on the same idea would not be.

slides.title: Reinvesting in growth
slides.text: Instead of spending all the profit right away, many entrepreneurs put some of it back into the business — better supplies, a nicer sign, more inventory. For example, if your bracelet business earns $20 profit one week, using $10 of it to buy more beads and string for next week (instead of spending it all on yourself) helps the business keep growing.

slides.title: Standing out from competitors
slides.text: If other people sell something similar, a business needs a reason customers should pick them — better quality, price, or service. For example, if three kids at your school are all selling friendship bracelets, offering custom colors made to order, or slightly better prices, gives customers a specific reason to choose you.

slides.title: Word of mouth
slides.text: Happy customers telling their friends is one of the most powerful (and free!) ways a small business grows. For example, if one classmate loves the bracelet you made them and shows five friends at lunch, you might suddenly have five new customers without spending a single cent on advertising.

slides.title: Building a name people remember
slides.text: A consistent name, look, or feel for your business — sometimes called a brand — helps customers recognize and trust you again next time. For example, always using the same logo sticker and the same colorful packaging for your bracelets helps customers instantly recognize "oh, that's from her bracelet business" when they see it.

slides.title: Selling online with help
slides.text: With a parent's help, some young entrepreneurs sell crafts or art through simple online marketplaces, reaching far more people than a stand on the street. For example, a 12-year-old who makes custom drawings might, with a parent's account and supervision, list a few pieces online and reach buyers far beyond just their own neighborhood.

slides.title: Pricing fairly
slides.text: Setting a fair price means charging enough to cover your costs and time, without charging so much that customers walk away. For example, if a bracelet costs $3 in materials to make, pricing it at $8 covers your costs and effort while still feeling fair to someone buying a handmade gift.

slides.title: Handling a dissatisfied customer
slides.text: How you respond when a customer is unhappy can matter more than the original mistake — a calm, fair fix often turns a complaint into loyalty. For example, if a customer says their custom mug arrived cracked, offering a free replacement instead of arguing about it usually keeps them as a customer instead of losing them for good.

slides.title: Marketing on a budget
slides.text: You don't need to spend much money to market a small business — social media posts, flyers, and word of mouth can all work well for free or cheap. For example, posting a few photos of your bracelets on a family member's social media account, tagged with your prices, can reach dozens of potential customers without spending a single dollar.

slides.title: Teamwork and clear agreements
slides.text: When you run a business with a partner, agreeing early on who does what and how profits get split helps avoid arguments later. For example, two friends running a dog-walking business might agree in writing that one handles scheduling and the other handles the actual walks, splitting profits evenly between them.

quiz.question: A dog-walking business earns $60 in a month but spends $75. Was that month a profit or a loss?
choices: A loss, since it spent more than it earned
A profit, since $60 sounds like a lot of money
quiz.explanation: A loss happens when costs are higher than what the business earns, even if the earnings sound decent on their own.

quiz.question: Why does it help to understand your customer?
choices: So you can offer what they actually want and can afford
It doesn't matter who buys your product
quiz.explanation: Knowing your customer helps you shape a product or service they'll actually want.

quiz.question: What does "reinvesting" mean?
choices: Putting some profit back into growing the business
Spending every bit of profit immediately
quiz.explanation: Reinvesting profit helps a business grow bigger and stronger over time.

quiz.question: Which is a "smart risk" for a young entrepreneur?
choices: Spending $10 of savings to try selling bracelets at a fair
Spending your entire year of savings on one untested idea
quiz.explanation: Smart entrepreneurs weigh risks carefully instead of risking everything blindly.

quiz.question: Three kids at school all sell friendship bracelets. Why might a business need to "stand out"?
choices: So customers have a reason to choose them specifically
Standing out never matters in business
quiz.explanation: If others sell something similar, standing out gives customers a reason to pick you.

quiz.question: What is "word of mouth"?
choices: Happy customers telling other people about a business
A type of advertisement you have to pay a lot for
quiz.explanation: Word of mouth is free, powerful marketing that comes from satisfied customers.

quiz.question: What is a "brand"?
choices: A consistent name or look that helps customers recognize a business
A random word with no meaning
quiz.explanation: A recognizable brand builds trust and makes customers more likely to return.

quiz.question: How might a young entrepreneur reach more customers than a street stand?
choices: Selling online with a parent's help
It's impossible to ever reach more people
quiz.explanation: Online marketplaces, used with a parent's guidance, can reach far more people than a physical stand.

quiz.question: A bracelet costs $3 in materials. Why might you price it at $8, not $20?
choices: It covers your costs and effort while still feeling fair to buyers
Higher prices are always better no matter what
quiz.explanation: A fair price balances covering your costs with what a customer is willing to pay.

quiz.question: A customer's mug arrives cracked. What response is most likely to keep them as a customer?
choices: A calm, fair fix, like a free replacement
Arguing that it's not your fault
quiz.explanation: Handling complaints calmly and fairly often turns an unhappy customer into a loyal one.

quiz.question: Why should business partners agree early on how profits will be split?
choices: It helps avoid arguments and confusion later
Profit splits never need to be discussed
quiz.explanation: A clear, upfront agreement keeps a partnership running smoothly as the business grows.

slides.title: What is a business plan?
slides.text: A business plan lays out what a business will sell, who it's for, how it'll make money, and what it needs to get started — a roadmap for turning an idea into reality. For example, a teen wanting to start a pet-sitting business might write a one-page plan covering who their customers are (nearby pet owners), how much they'll charge per visit, and what supplies (a leash, treats, a scheduling app) they need first.

slides.title: Startup vs. small business
slides.text: A small business often grows steadily and stays similar in size. A startup usually aims to grow very fast, often testing a new idea that hasn't been proven yet. For example, a local pet-sitting business run by one teen is a small business, growing steadily one customer at a time — while an app trying to connect thousands of pet owners with sitters nationwide, aiming to grow fast, would be more like a startup.

slides.title: Where funding comes from
slides.text: Businesses can be funded with personal savings, loans, or investors who give money in exchange for a share of future profits or ownership. For example, a teen might use $50 of their own savings to buy initial supplies, while a bigger startup might convince an investor to provide $50,000 in exchange for owning 10% of the company.

slides.title: What does "scaling" mean?
slides.text: Scaling means growing a business to serve many more customers without everything becoming proportionally more expensive or difficult to manage. For example, a tutoring business that only earns more by adding more of the tutor's own hours doesn't scale well, but selling a recorded video course that hundreds of students can buy without extra work per student scales much better.

slides.title: Failure is part of the process
slides.text: Many successful entrepreneurs failed at a first (or second, or third) attempt. Learning from what went wrong is often what makes the next attempt succeed. For example, a teen's first attempt at selling custom phone cases online might flop due to poor photos and unclear pricing — but applying those exact lessons to a second attempt often leads to real success.

slides.title: Ethics in business
slides.text: Long-term success usually depends on being honest with customers, treating employees fairly, and not cutting corners just to make a quick profit. For example, honestly describing a product's condition, even when a vague description might sell it faster, builds the kind of trust that keeps customers coming back for years.

slides.title: Solving a real problem
slides.text: The most durable businesses tend to solve a genuine problem for people — not just chase a trend that might fade quickly. For example, a tutoring business solving a real, ongoing need (students struggling with math) tends to last far longer than a business built around a fad that's popular for a few months and then forgotten.

slides.title: Resilience and persistence
slides.text: Markets change, plans fail, and competitors appear. Entrepreneurs who adapt and keep going tend to outlast those who give up at the first setback. For example, if a new competitor undercuts your prices, adapting by improving your service or finding a new customer niche is more likely to succeed than simply giving up.

slides.title: Businesses that also help others
slides.text: Some entrepreneurs build 'social enterprises' — businesses designed to make money while also solving a social or environmental problem, not purely for profit. For example, a teen-run business that sells reusable water bottles and donates a portion of every sale to a clean-water charity is pursuing both profit and positive impact at the same time.

slides.title: Measuring success beyond money
slides.text: Revenue matters, but many entrepreneurs also track customer satisfaction, repeat business, and real-world impact as signs their business is genuinely succeeding. For example, a business that earns a modest profit but has 90% of customers coming back again and again is arguably in a stronger position than one earning more but constantly losing and replacing one-time customers.

slides.title: Pricing strategies
slides.text: Businesses generally price in one of two ways: cost-plus pricing, where you add a markup on top of what something costs to make, or value-based pricing, where you charge based on how much a customer believes it's worth. For example, a $5 material cost with a $10 markup gives a cost-plus price of $15, while a designer bag might sell for $200 largely because customers value the brand, not just the materials.

slides.title: Handling complaints and protecting your reputation
slides.text: A single public complaint, especially online, can influence far more potential customers than just the one person who made it, so how a business responds matters enormously. For example, a business that quickly and openly resolves a customer's shipping complaint often earns more trust from onlookers than a business that has never had a complaint at all.

slides.title: Customer acquisition and marketing spend
slides.text: Customer acquisition cost is how much money a business spends, on average, to gain one new customer through advertising, and it needs to stay lower than what that customer is expected to spend over time. For example, spending $20 on ads to gain a customer who only ever buys $15 worth of products is a losing strategy, even if the ads technically "worked."

slides.title: Splitting equity among co-founders
slides.text: When multiple people start a company together, they typically divide ownership — called equity — based on factors like who contributed the original idea, how much money each person invested, and how much ongoing work each will do. For example, two co-founders might split equity 50/50 if they contribute equally, or 70/30 if one invested significantly more money or works full-time while the other stays part-time.

quiz.question: What is a business plan?
choices: A roadmap covering what a business will sell, who it's for, and how it makes money
A legal document required only for huge companies
quiz.explanation: A business plan turns a rough idea into a structured, actionable roadmap.

quiz.question: How does a startup typically differ from a small business?
choices: A startup usually aims to grow very fast with an unproven idea
There is no real difference between them
quiz.explanation: Startups often chase fast, unproven growth; small businesses often grow more steadily.

quiz.question: An investor gives $50,000 in exchange for 10% ownership. What did they get?
choices: A share of future profits or ownership
Nothing at all, ever
quiz.explanation: Investors typically fund a business in exchange for equity or a share of future returns.

quiz.question: Why does a recorded video course "scale" better than one-on-one tutoring?
choices: It can serve many more customers without proportionally more cost or effort
Video courses are always cheaper to make
quiz.explanation: Scaling is about growing efficiently, not just growing bigger at any cost.

quiz.question: Why do many successful entrepreneurs talk openly about past failures?
choices: Learning from what went wrong often shapes what succeeds next
Failure has no useful lessons at all
quiz.explanation: Failure is frequently a genuine part of the path to eventual success.

quiz.question: Why does ethical behavior matter for long-term business success?
choices: Cutting corners for quick profit tends to damage trust over time
Ethics have no real impact on whether a business succeeds
quiz.explanation: Businesses built on trust and fairness tend to last longer than ones that cut corners.

quiz.question: What tends to make a business durable over the long run?
choices: Solving a genuine, ongoing problem for people
Only ever chasing whatever trend is popular right now
quiz.explanation: Businesses solving real, lasting problems tend to outlast those chasing short-lived trends.

quiz.question: What is a "social enterprise"?
choices: A business built to make money while also solving a social or environmental problem
A business that only exists on social media
quiz.explanation: Social enterprises intentionally pursue impact alongside profit.

quiz.question: Besides revenue, what else might an entrepreneur track as a sign of success?
choices: Customer satisfaction and real-world impact
Nothing else is ever worth tracking
quiz.explanation: Many entrepreneurs value signs of genuine success beyond just the money earned.

quiz.question: What's the difference between cost-plus and value-based pricing?
choices: Cost-plus adds a markup to cost; value-based charges based on perceived worth
They are exactly the same thing
quiz.explanation: The two strategies anchor a price to different things: your cost, or the customer's perceived value.

quiz.question: Why does responding well to a public complaint matter so much?
choices: It's visible to many potential customers, not just the one who complained
Public complaints never affect other customers
quiz.explanation: Onlookers judge a business by how it handles problems, not just whether problems happen.

quiz.question: A business spends $20 to gain a customer who only spends $15. What's the problem?
choices: The cost of acquiring that customer is higher than what they spend
There is no problem at all
quiz.explanation: If customer acquisition cost exceeds what a customer spends, that growth actually loses money.
